Industry News: Mastering Long Contexts in LLMs with KVPress

📅 23 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR: KVPress packs the latest KV cache compression techniques, enabling memory-efficient long-context LLMs.
  • In a recent development, one of the key features of Large Language Models (LLMs) is their context window—the maximum number of tokens they can process in a single request.
  • Larger context windows unlock incredible possibilities:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: KVPress packs the latest KV cache compression techniques, enabling memory-efficient long-context LLMs. 🚀.

In a recent development, one of the key features of Large Language Models (LLMs) is their context window—the maximum number of tokens they can process in a single request. As LLMs evolve, their context windows are becoming increasingly larger.

Larger context windows unlock incredible possibilities:.

However, these extended windows come at a cost—memory taken by the long context in the KV Cache becomes hard to manage. For instance, handling 1M tokens with Llama 3-70B in float16 demands 330GB for KV Cache, rendering it infeasible for many applications.

In this blog post, we'll address one solution for this problem: compressing the KV Cache for more efficient generation. To achieve this, we'll explore:.

Before getting started, explore KVPress in this Space (you'll find examples at the end if needed):.

Figure 1: Key Value cache inside the attention module (Source: NVIDIA).

In autoregressive models, text generation happens token by token, with each prediction relying on all preceding tokens for context. For example:.

It has been revealed that this repetitive computation becomes inefficient as the sequence grows, especially for large models. KV Cache optimizes this process by storing the intermediate results—keys (K) and values (V)—from the attention layers, so the model can reuse them for future tokens instead of recalculating them.

As powerful as the KV Cache is, it comes with a major drawback-it scales linearly with the size of the context window. While this might not sound alarming at first, let's break it down to see why this becomes a serious bottleneck.

In a recent development, the values stored in the KV Cache come from all the attention blocks used by the model. Therefore, its size depends on the model architecture, which dictates the number of attention heads. More concretely, the memory consumed by the KV Cache is determined by the following equation:.

Size(KV)=2×precision×nlayers×nheads×d×ntokens \text{Size}(\text{KV}) = 2 \times \text{precision} \times n_{layers} \times n_{heads} \times d \times n_{tokens} Size(KV)=2×precision×nlayers​×nheads​×d×ntokens​.

Industry observers note that each of these factors contributes to the explosion in memory usage. To make this more tangible, let's consider a concrete example—Llama 3-70B running in bfloat16 precision (as recommended by the model authors) with a context size of 1M tokens:.

Size(KV)=2×2×80×8×128×1M=327.6GB \text{Size}(\text{KV}) = 2 \times 2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 1M = 327.6 \text{GB} Size(KV)=2×2×80×8×128×1M=327.6GB.

In a recent development, since bfloat16 uses 2 bytes per parameter, the model weights alone require 140 GB (70B x 2 bytes). This means that running the model with a 1M token context size demands approximately 470 GB of memory, with the KV cache alone accounting for a staggering 70% of this total.

Sources indicate that as we've seen, the KV Cache is both a critical enabler and a significant bottleneck for deploying large language models (LLMs) with long context windows. Addressing the linearly scaling memory problem requires innovative compression techniques, and that's exactly where KVPress steps in.

It has been revealed that KVPress, developed by NVIDIA, is a Python toolkit designed to address the memory challenges of large KV Caches by providing a suite of state-of-the-art compression techniques. It also integrates with other approaches, such as KV Cache Quantization, a method built into the transformers library to reduce memory usage (the precision term in the equation above), further expanding its utility (details here).

For researchers specializing in compression, KVPress offers a flexible and modular framework, making it easy to understand and extend with new methods. For developers, KVPress simplifies the process of deploying these cutting-edge techniques, enabling quick and efficient integration into real-world applications.

At its core, KVPress leverages presses, which are advanced compression algorithms specifically designed to reduce the memory footprint of the KV Cache.

Many of these presses rely on a score that is used in each head to prune the KV pairs with the lowest importance. For instance the KnormPress prunes the KV pairs with lowest key value norm (paper), and SnapKVPress prunes the KV pairs associated with a low attention weights for the latest queries (paper).

These presses are seamlessly integrated into the attention layers of the model using forward hooks.

Figure 2: KV Compression visualized (Source: NVIDIA).

During text generation, they dynamically compress the KV Cache, reducing memory usage without compromising the model's ability to generate coherent and accurate outputs. Each press is characterized by a compression_ratio attribute, which determines the degree of compression applied to the KV Cache.

These presses integrate seamlessly with a custom transformers pipeline, enabling easy application and experimentation.

It has been revealed that here's how you can use a press with KVPress with one of the many presses, ExpectedAttentionPress. This press prunes the KV pairs associated with the lowest expected attention weight for future queries.

Try using it directly in this Hugging Face space or in this Google colab notebook!

By targeting the pre-filling phase, KVPress ensures that the cache is compressed when it's largest—helping reduce memory overhead for sequences with tens of thousands or even millions of tokens.

The plot below demonstrates the GPU memory savings achieved with KVPress compression as prompt lengths increase. For shorter prompts, most of the memory is allocated to model weights—approximately 15GB for Llama 3.1 8B in bfloat16. However, as prompt lengths grow, the KV cache becomes a major contributor to memory consumption. For 128k context length, applying KVPress with a 50% compression ratio reduces peak memory usage from 45GB to 37GB. This smaller KV cache also improves decoding speed, from 11 tokens per second to 17 tokens per second on an A100 GPU (source). .

Figure 3: Memory usage vs Context length (Source: NVIDIA).

Industry observers note that the research community has been actively developing various techniques for KV cache compression. KVPress encourages researchers to contribute their methods and already provides more than a dozen presses.

To evaluate the performance of these presses, KVPress includes a simple CLI for benchmarking them on standard long-context datasets such as RULER, InfiniteBench, and Loogle. The plot below benchmarks 9 different presses on the RULER dataset with 4k context length and different compression ratio. The best performing press on this dataset is a combination of the AdaKVPress (paper) and ExpectedAttentionPress, a fresh unpublished pruning technique created by the authors of KVPress (more information here).

Figure 4: Average score vs Compression ratio (Source: NVIDIA).

It has been revealed that the growing context windows of LLMs unlock latest possibilities but pose significant memory challenges with the linearly scaling KV Cache. KVPress addresses this by compressing the cache during the critical pre-filling phase.

According to recent reports, while KVPress improves memory efficiency, higher compression ratios can impact model accuracy, as shown in the benchmark plot. Further research is needed to develop more effective compression algorithms that minimize trade-offs.

Sources indicate that with its seamless integration into the transformers library and modular design, KVPress empowers researchers and developers to handle long-context LLMs efficiently and design upcoming compression techniques. It's a practical solution for scaling LLMs without overwhelming memory resources—ensuring innovation stays accessible as models grow.

  • We have added vision support to smolagents, which unlocks the use of vision language models in agentic pipelines natively.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, you hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye. Matthew 7, 3-5.

We have added vision support to smolagents, which unlocks the use of vision language models in agentic pipelines natively.

Industry observers note that in the agentic world, many capabilities are hidden behind a vision wall. A common example is web browsing: web pages feature rich visual content that you never fully recover by simply extracting their text, be it the relative position of objects, messages transmitted through color, specific icons… In this case, vision is a real superpower for agents. So we just added this capability to our smolagents!

Teaser of what this gives: an agentic browser that navigates the web in complete autonomy!

Here's an example of what it looks like:.

🤔 How do we want to pass images to agents? Passing an image can be done in two ways:.

For the case where we want to pass images at once, we added the possibility to pass a list of images to the agent in the run method: agent.run("Describe these images:", images=[image_1, image_2]) .

These image inputs are then stored in the task_images attribute of TaskStep along with the prompt of the task that you'd like to accomplish.

Industry observers note that when running the agent, they will be passed to the model. This comes in handy with cases like taking actions based on long PDFs that include visual elements.

How to dynamically add images into the agent’s memory?

To find out, we first need to understand how our agents work.

All agents in smolagents are based on the singular MultiStepAgent class, which is an abstraction of the ReAct framework. On a basic level, this class performs actions on a cycle of following steps, where existing variables and knowledge are incorporated into the agent logs as follows:.

The figure below details this process:.

As you can see, for use cases where images are dynamically retrieved (e.g. web browser agent), we support adding images to the model’s ActionStep, in attribute step_log.observation_images.

This can be done via a callback, which will be run at the end of each step.

Let's demonstrate how to make such a callback, and using it to build a web browser agent.👇👇.

In a recent development, we’re going to use helium. It provides browser automations based on selenium: this will be an easier way for our agent to manipulate webpages.

The agent itself can use helium directly, so no need for specific tools: it can directly use helium to perform actions, such as click("top 10") to click the button named "top 10" visible on the page. We still have to make some tools to help the agent navigate the web: a tool to go back to the previous page, and another tool to close pop-ups, because these are quite hard to grab for helium since they don’t have any text on their close buttons.

For now, the agent has no visual input. So let us demonstrate how to dynamically feed it images in its step logs by using a callback. We make a callback save_screenshot that will be run at the end of each step.

The most important line here is when we add the image in our observations images: step_log.observations_images = [image.copy()].

This callback accepts both the step_log, and the agent itself as arguments. Having agent as an input allows to perform deeper operations than just modifying the last logs.

In a recent development, let's make a model. We've added support for images in all models. Just one precision: when using TransformersModel with a VLM, for it to work properly you need to pass flatten_messages_as_text as False upon initialization, like:.

For this demo, let's use a bigger Qwen2VL via Fireworks API:.

Sources indicate that now let’s move on to defining our agent. We set the highest verbosity_level to display the LLM’s full output messages to view its thoughts, and we increased max_steps to 20 to give the agent more steps to explore the web. We also provide it with our callback save_screenshot defined above.

Finally, we provide our agent with some guidance about using helium.

Now everything's ready: Let’s run our agent!

Note, however, that this task is really hard: depending on the VLM that you use, this might not always work. Strong VLMs like Qwen2VL-72B or GPT-4o succeed more often.

This will give you a glimpse of the capabilities of a vision-enabled CodeAgent, but there’s much more to do!

We are looking forward to seeing what you will build with vision language models and smolagents!

Note: for the modal closing selectors please note that modals are also known as dialog elements and if built robustly should have a role="dialog" attribute in this is something that can be searched for when identifying these pop up windows.

In addition, any dialog/modal window should be closeable via the escape key as well!

Hope this helps identify modals/dialogs in a broader sense and/or helps close them out easier!

How to Build an AI-Assisted Workflow That Does Not Leak

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1388 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • According to recent reports, 7 Day Free Trial.
  • It has been revealed that A generative AI tool can draft a client email, summarise a forty-message thread or refactor a function in seconds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sources indicate that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

According to recent reports, 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

It has been revealed that A generative AI tool can draft a client email, summarise a forty-message thread or refactor a function in seconds. That speed is real, and it explains how fast these tools have become part of the ordinary working day, used to summarise threads, draft replies and reformat data in a single paste. The same ease is the problem. It moves sensitive material into systems that were never scoped to hold it, quietly and at scale.

Sources indicate that here is the uncomfortable part for anyone running a lean team. The risk in that workflow is almost never the model being wrong. It is that nobody decided what should go into the tool in the first place, and nobody is accountable for where the data ends up. AI made the drafting instant. It did nothing on its own to make delegation safe.

It has been revealed that this article is about the control that closes that gap. It is not a product and it is not a policy document. It is a person, placed deliberately in the workflow, making the one call that no model can make for you.

Samsung learned this in public. In 2023, engineers in its semiconductor division were given access to ChatGPT to help debug source code. Within weeks, staff had pasted proprietary code and internal meeting notes into the tool, and Samsung banned generative AI across the organization soon after. The story ran everywhere, from Bloomberg to The Register. Nothing malfunctioned. People simply moved sensitive material into a system that was never scoped to hold it, and the material was gone.

Two things make this failure mode easy to hit, and both are structural rather than careless.

It has been revealed that first, most of these tools run in the browser. The data loss prevention software a security team relies on was built to watch files, endpoints and network egress, and it often cannot see a paste action into a web app at all. Worse, much of this activity happens through personal accounts that sit outside the controls the organisation does have. The leak does not trip an alarm because nothing was downloaded and nothing was emailed. Text was typed into a box.

Recent findings suggest that second, consumer-grade accounts can retain what you give them. OpenAI's own documentation states that content from consumer ChatGPT may be used to improve its models unless the user turns that setting off. Paste a client list or a contract clause from the wrong account, and that material may now sit inside a training pipeline you do not control and cannot claw back.

For a developer or a founder, the lesson is not "do not use AI". It is that the point of failure sits one layer above the model, in how the work is handed off and who decided what was safe to hand over.

Industry observers note that if any of the data moving through that workflow identifies a person, a client, a candidate, an employee or an investor, then GDPR treats the tools and people touching it as processors acting on your behalf. That sounds abstract until you translate it into design constraints, which is what a technical team can actually work with.

Under Article 28 of the GDPR, anyone who processes personal data for you must do so under a binding contract that sets out what is processed, for what purpose and for how long, and everyone handling that data must be under a confidentiality commitment. An AI vendor you have never papered is a processor you have not accounted for. A free account used quietly by one engineer is a sub-processor nobody signed off. The obligation does not disappear because the tool was convenient.

Location is the second constraint, and it is the one most teams miss. A person, contractor or tool processing your data outside the EU means personal data is being transferred outside the EU, which requires a specific safeguard such as the Standard Contractual Clauses on top of the Article 28 contract. Keep the procesing inside the EU and that entire category of transfer risk falls away before you have to manage it. For UK teams the position is the same: the Information Commissioner's Office sets out the identical core terms for a processor contract, documented instructions, confidentiality, security measures, rules on sub-processors, and deletion or return of data at the end of the engagement.

Sources indicate that there is now a second regulatory layer as well. The EU AI Act, which entered into force in 2024, adds obligations on how AI systems are deployed and governed, on top of the data-protection duties GDPR already imposes. The detail is still settling, but the direction is clear: unmanaged, undocumented AI use is getting harder to defend, not easier. None of this is exotic. It is the same governance you would apply to any third party with access to your systems. AI simply introduced a new processor that most workflows never wrote down.

According to recent reports, "Human in the loop" usually gets discussed as a quality measure: a person checks the output so errors do not ship. That is true, and it undersells the point badly. The human is also the only part of the workflow that can make a judgment about what should never enter the tool at all.

A model cannot decide that a board deck stays out of a consumer chatbot. A browser extension cannot know that one folder holds client data governed by a contract that forbids sub-processing without written consent. Those are judgment calls, and judgment is precisely the thing you cannot automate. The person doing the delegating is your policy enforcement point, sitting at the exact moment the decision is made. They decide what gets pasted, what gets redacted first, what runs only inside an enterprise account with training switched off, and what a human handles end to end because the risk is simply not worth the minutes saved.

This reframes the division of labour that actually holds up. The AI owns the mechanical layer: summarising a long thread, turning rough notes into a first draft, extracting action items, reformatting data. The human owns the judgment layer: what matters, how it is framed, and, above all, where the data is allowed to go. Remove the human and you have not automated the work. You have removed the only control that was reading the situation and deciding what was safe.

It is worth being specific about what that judgment looks like in practice, because it is a skill and not a job title. Someone exercising it knows which inputs are off limits without having to ask, keeps sensitive material inside controlled systems by default, and treats the question "should this go into the tool at all" as part of the work rather than an afterthought. Whether that person is an engineer, an operations lead or an executive assistant, the control is the same: someone with enough context to know what is sensitive, and enough standing to say no. That habit is what separates a workflow that is genuinely governed from one that merely has a policy document nobody reads.

The practical version, for a founder or a small technical team that wants the speed without the exposure:.

According to recent reports, most teams can put the first four in place in about a week. The last two are harder, because they are not configuration changes. They are about whether the workflow still holds when the people in it change, and that is the part most teams discover they got wrong only after someone has already left.

In a recent development, the speed of AI is not in question. What AI cannot supply is the judgment about what should enter it, and the accountability for where the output goes. Treat the human in the loop as a security control, design the workflow around that control, and you keep the nine-second draft without the quiet data leak. Remove the human, and the only thing you have really automated is the leak.

It has been revealed that openAI’s Sora demo marked a striking advance in AI-generated video last year and gave us a glimpse of the potential capabilities of video generation models. The impact was immediate and since that demo, the video generation space has become increasingly competitive with major players and startups producing their own highly capable models such as Google’s Veo2, Haliluo’s Minimax, Runway’s Gen3 Alpha, Kling, Pika, and Luma Lab’s Dream Machine.

Open-source has also had its own surge of video generation models with CogVideoX, Mochi-1, Hunyuan, Allegro, and LTX Video. Is the video community having its “Stable Diffusion moment”?

This post will provide a brief overview of the state of video generation models, where we are with respect to open video generation models, and how the Diffusers team is planning to support their adoption at scale.

These are today's most popular video models for AI-generated content creation.

There are several factors we’d like to see and control in videos:.

Sources indicate that with image generation models, we usually only care about the first three aspects. However, for video generation we now have to consider motion quality, coherence and consistency over time, potentially with multiple subjects. Finding the right balance between good data, right inductive priors, and training methodologies to suit these additional requirements has proved to be more challenging than other modalities.

Text-to-video generation models have similar components as their text-to-image counterparts:.

The latest generation of video models shares a core feature where the denoising network processes 3D video tokens that capture both spatial and temporal information. The video encoder-decoder system, responsible for producing and decoding these tokens, employs both spatial and temporal compression. While decoding the latents typically demands the most memory, these models offer frame-by-frame decoding options to reduce memory usage.

In a recent development, text conditioning is incorporated through either joint attention (introduced in Stable Diffusion 3) or cross-attention. T5 has emerged as the preferred text encoder across most models, with HunYuan being an exception in its use of both CLIP-L and LLaMa 3.

The denoising network itself builds on the DiT architecture developed by William Peebles and Saining Xie, while incorporating various design elements from PixArt.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you’ve ever struggled with a tough math problem, you know how useful it is to think a little longer and work through it carefully. OpenAI’s o1 model revealed that when LLMs are trained to do the same—by using more compute during inference—they get significantly better at solving reasoning tasks like mathematics, coding, and logic.

However, the recipe behind OpenAI’s reasoning models has been a well kept secret. That is, until last week, when DeepSeek released their DeepSeek-R1 model and promptly broke the internet (and the stock market!).

Besides performing as well or better than o1, the DeepSeek-R1 release was accompanied by a detailed tech report that outlined the key steps of their training recipe. This recipe involved several innovations, most notably the application of pure reinforcement learning to teach a base language model how to reason without any human supervision. As shown in the figure below, making a powerful reasoning model is now very simple if you have access to a capable base model and a high-quality data mixture:.

However, the DeepSeek-R1 release leaves open several questions about:.

These questions prompted us to launch the Open-R1 project, an initiative to systematically reconstruct DeepSeek-R1’s data and training pipeline, validate its claims, and push the boundaries of open reasoning models. By building Open-R1, we aim to provide transparency on how reinforcement learning can enhance reasoning, share reproducible insights with the open-source community, and create a foundation for future models to leverage these techniques.

In this blog post we take a look at key ingredients behind DeepSeek-R1, which parts we blueprint to replicate, and how to contribute to the Open-R1 project.

DeepSeek-R1 is a reasoning model built on the foundation of DeepSeek-V3. Like any good reasoning model, it starts with a strong base model, and DeepSeek-V3 is exactly that. This 671B Mixture of Experts (MoE) model performs on par with heavyweights like Sonnet 3.5 and GPT-4o. What’s especially impressive is how cost-efficient it was to train—just $5.5M—thanks to architectural changes like Multi Token Prediction (MTP), Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) and a LOT (seriously, a lot) of hardware optimization.

Industry observers note that deepSeek also introduced two models: DeepSeek-R1-Zero and DeepSeek-R1, each with a distinct training approach. DeepSeek-R1-Zero skipped supervised fine-tuning altogether and relied entirely on reinforcement learning (RL), using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to make the process more efficient. A simple reward system was used to guide the model, providing feedback based on the accuracy and structure of its answers. This approach helped the model develop useful reasoning skills, such as breaking problems into steps and verifying its own outputs. However, its responses often lacked clarity and were difficult to read.

Industry observers note that that’s where DeepSeek-R1 comes in. It started with a "cold start" phase, fine-tuning on a small set of carefully crafted examples to improve clarity and readability. From there, it went through more RL and refinement steps, including rejecting low-quality outputs with both human preference based and verifiable reward, to create a model that not only reasons well but also produces polished and consistent answers.

Industry observers note that this all sounds great, but what's actually missing? Let's have a look at the missing pieces of the puzzle.

The release of DeepSeek-R1 is an amazing boon for the community, but they didn’t release everything—although the model weights are open, the datasets and code used to train the model are not 😢.

Industry observers note that the goal of Open-R1 is to build these last missing pieces so that the whole research and industry community can build similar or better models using these recipes and datasets. And by doing this in the open, everybody in the community can contribute!

As shown in the figure below, here’s our plan of attack:.

Sources indicate that note that we don’t want to stop at math datasets. There’s a lot of potential in exploring other areas, obvious one like code but also scientific fields such as medicine, where reasoning models could have significant impact.

Industry observers note that this initiative isn’t just about replicating results—it’s about sharing insights with the community. By documenting what works, what doesn’t, and why, we hope to save others from wasting time and compute on unproductive paths.

If this sounds interesting, we’d love your help! Whether it’s contributing code, joining discussions on Hugging Face, there are plenty of ways to get involved. Let’s build this together! 🚀.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that today, we are launching the integration of four awesome serverless Inference Providers – fal, Replicate, Sambanova, Together AI – directly on the Hub’s model pages. They are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for JS and Python), making it easier than ever to explore serverless inference of a wide variety of models that run on your favorite providers.

In a recent development, we’ve been hosting a serverless Inference API on the Hub for a long time (we introduced the v1 in summer 2020 – wow, time flies 🤯). While this has enabled easy exploration and prototyping, we’ve refined our core value proposition towards collaboration, storage, versioning, and distribution of large datasets and models with the community. At the same time, serverless providers have flourished, and the time was right for Hugging Face to offer easy and unified access to serverless inference through a set of great providers.

Just as we work with great partners like AWS, Nvidia and others for dedicated deployment options via the model pages’ Deploy button, it was natural to partner with the next generation of serverless inference providers for model-centric, serverless inference.

Here’s what this enables, taking the timely example of DeepSeek-ai/DeepSeek-R1, a model which has achieved mainstream fame over the past few days 🔥:.

Rodrigo Liang, Co-Founder & CEO at SambaNova: "We are excited to be partnering with Hugging Face to accelerate its Inference API. Hugging Face developers now have access to much faster inference speeds on a wide range of the best open source models.".

Sources indicate that zeke Sikelianos, Founding Designer at Replicate: "Hugging Face is the de facto home of open-source model weights, and has been a key player in making AI more accessible to the world. We use Hugging Face internally at Replicate as our weights registry of choice, and we're honored to be among the first inference providers to be featured in this launch.".

This is just the start, and we’ll build on top of this with the community in the coming weeks!

This turn might not seem like that major of a deal to many of you... But in practice, this very clearly constitutes an abrupt cutting-off of the lion's share of the quasi-subsidized compute erstwhile accessible through HF.

And though seldom overtly publicized as a core feature of the platform, that nonchalantly encouraging compute reservoir of yore (even if accessible only via select pockets, like Inference Endpoints) served for years as a kind of a phantom fertilizer, and a key one, for Machine Learning adoption, experimentation, and resource-strapped development – on par with other quasi-subsidized resources like Google Colab and ChatGPT . And it's entirely plausible that the availability of such resources en masse has been the single most vital prerequisite, as well as mandatory catalyst, for the continual evolution/democratization of open source ML specifically, whether in regards to utility or literacy or safety or any other oft-evoked marker, and in some large part the popularization of ML more broadly.

Of course, despite its qualitative obviousness, the impact of subsidized resources may be difficult, maybe impossible, to summate objectively or to quantify directly. After all they constitute a set of infrastructures the immediate production of which tends to assume forms that are often ephemeral, social – like practices, understanding, or values – and wherever concrete, often non-commercial, like open models, adapters, enthusiast contributions, articles, posts, etc. And by the markers of finance and markets, such productions may be deemed as having only a tangential value to, say, the capitalization potential of a given platform, all-the-while adding heavy and at times unforeseeably fluctuating costs upkeep.

Nonetheless, (and there are few better illustrations for this than ML) public access to subsidized resources persisting in open forms (non-transactional, nor overtly monetized, nor strictly delimited: like all public resources, services, libraries, spaces) simultaneously remains a key precondition for the economic and socio-cultural potential of the entire technological and research field as a whole, whilst continually stimulating the range and variety of forms this potential may ultimately assume.

In a recent development, as recently as a year ago, I would avidly preach the merits of Huggingface to everyone I know: not only as the key extant firmament for humanist and democratized machine learning paradigms to emerge and thrive upon, but as a really-existing pre-figuration of a new form of society, one that may at last transcend the intertwined logic of alienation, separation, disparity, scarcity, disposability, amnesia, exploitation, and all the rest of it... That's what I used to associate with Huggingface. Nowadays though: I think of Huggingface, and my next thought is "$2.00".

I know that for resources or platforms to remain subsidized, such subsidies must come from someplace. And assuring reliable funding may be a challenge, especially these days. Nonetheless, I really believe that it would be a grave mistake long-term for HF to rely on standard transactional/commercial monetization sourced from its consumers, even to cover real costs (much less to extract surplus "value" from or for anyone). To best serve its role within the field, HF must instead move closer to operating as a non-profit, sourcing unconditional funding from elsewhere , with the assumption that it may always operate at a "loss", whilst playing a key role in the thriving and the dynamism of the field as a whole.

Hugging Face Inference Endpoints offers an easy and secure way to deploy Machine Learning models on dedicated compute for use in production on AWS. You no longer need to build a dashboard every time you want to investigate a drop in traffic or compare campaign results. With servers built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), you can ask an AI assistant a question and let it retrieve the relevant data directly from your marketing tools.

According to recent reports, but connecting an assistant to Google Analytics is not the same as connecting it to HubSpot or Ahrefs. Each server exposes different data, capabilities and levels of access. Some are built for quick analysis inside one platform, while others support reporting across several channels. This guide compares four servers, what they can do, how they are set up and where their limits matter. Details such as looks and tool lists change often, so confirm them against each vendor's documentation before you commit.

The summary below reflects each vendor's documentation at the time of writing.

Google publishes an official, open-source Google Analytics MCP server for GA4. It connects AI assistants to the Admin and Data APIs, so it can list accounts and properties, run standard, realtime, funnel and conversion reports, and inspect custom dimensions and metrics. That makes it useful for investigating traffic changes, landing page performance and engagement trends.

Example prompt: "Which landing pages lost the most engaged sessions this month compared with last month?" The assistant can pull the relevant reports and help you spot changes, and you can then check whether the decline comes from specific channels, countries or devices.

Setup: The server runs locally. Google's documentation lists Python 3.10 or later, pipx or uvx, a Google Cloud project with the Analytics Admin and Data APIs enabled, application default credentials with the read-only Analytics scope, and at least Viewer access on the property you want to query.

Access: Google describes the server as available for read requests only, so it cannot change your Analytics configuration.

Limitations: It covers GA4 only, so it cannot combine website metrics with CRM records or advertising costs on its own. Running it locally also means you maintain the configuration yourself.

Best for: Web analysts and technical marketers who regularly investigate GA4 performance.

In a recent development, marketing performance usually spans several platforms. Google Ads generates clicks, GA4 tracks site activity and a CRM records leads. Seeing the whole picture means bringing those metrics together.

Recent findings suggest that coupler is a no-code data integration platform that offers MCP access to prepared business data. It lists more than 400 supported data sources, including Google Ads, Facebook Ads, GA4, HubSpot, LinkedIn Ads and Shopify, and lets teams combine and transform data before an assistant queries it.

Example prompt: "What was our cost per lead across Google Ads, Meta Ads and LinkedIn last quarter?" For paid search specifically, Coulper describes a Google Ads MCP server that lets you ask about campaigns and compare them with other connected channels.

Setup: Coupler is hosted, so there is nothing to install locally. You connect your platforms, configure data flows, choose refresh schedules and connect a compatible AI assistant. According to the vendor, queries run against the prepared datasets, which is useful for recurring reports because teams can reuse refreshed data instead of preparing exports by hand.

Limitations: Answers depend on the data included in your configured flows. Strategy requirements and privacy options can vary by subscription, so check the current plan details before you rely on it.

Best for: Agencies and teams that need consistent reporting across advertising, website analytics, ecommerce and CRM platforms.

According to recent reports, hubSpot's remote MCP server became generally available on April 13, 2026. It connects compatible AI clients to CRM data such as contacts, companies, deals, tickets and activities, and can also read marketing objects such as campaigns, landing pages and blog posts. That helps marketers investigate lead quality, pipeline performance and lifecycle trends without reviewing records one by one.

Example prompt: "Which deals created last quarter originated from webinar leads, and how many closed?" The assistant can retrieve the records and examine conversion patterns, provided the attribution data exists.

Setup: HubSpot hosts the server. In your account you create an MCP auth app under Development, then connect an MCP client that supports OAuth 2.1 with PKCE to the HubSpot endpoint. See HubSpot's remote MCP server documentation for current steps.

Access: Unlike a purely analytical server, HubSpot supports selected create and patch actions on records such as contacts, companies, deals, tickets and activities. Other objects, including marketing content, are read-only.

Limitations: Available operations differ by object type, and incomplete lead sources or inconsistent lifecycle stages will weaken any analysis.

Best for: B2B marketers and revenue operations teams that manage customers and pipeline in HubSpot.

Ahrefs offers a hosted MCP server that brings its SEO data into compatible assistants. It supports conversational research into keywords, backlinks, competing pages and organic visibility, so you can follow up with questions instead of exporting report after report.

Example prompt: "Which websites link to both of our main competitors but don't link to us?" The assistant can retrieve backlink data and help you identify outreach targets, which you can then narrow by Domain Rating or organic traffic.

Setup: According to the Ahrefs MCP documentation, the remote server is available on paid prepares starting from Lite, and you authorize it through your AI client. Ahrefs also publishes a getting started guide.

Limitations: Calls made through MCP use your monthly API units in the same way as direct API usage, and rows per request depend on your initiative. Ahrefs documents a default cap of 200,000 units per month for keys created through OAuth, which workspace admins can change. The data is also SEO-focused rather than first-party conversion analytics.

Best for: SEO specialists, content marketers and link builders who already use Ahrefs.

Sources indicate that yes, but start with the connections your team actually needs. Each additional server adds tools the assistant has to choose between, which increases complexity. Combining Ahrefs and HubSpot, for example, supports separate SEO and CRM investigations, but connecting several servers does not automatically create a reliable cross-platform reporting system.

Recent findings suggest that for recurring reports, prepare consistent datasets and validate the first results against your existing dashboards. That catches errors caused by mismatched metrics or attribution rules.

In a recent development, are MCP servers safe for marketing data? Security depends on the provider, the authentication method and the permissions you grant. Use trusted servers, review access scopes, and enable write operations only when necessary.

Sources indicate that do I need coding skills to use MCP servers? Not necessarily. Hosted services usually need less configuration, while local servers such as Google's need extra setup.

Which AI clients support MCP? Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor and other tools support MCP connections, though functionality and setup differ.

Do MCP servers cost extra? It depends on the provider. Some require paid looks, and others consume API credits or have usage limits.

It has been revealed that pick the server that matches the question you ask most often: Google Analytics MCP for GA4 behavior, Coupler for cross-channel reporting, HubSpot for CRM and lifecycle analysis, and Ahrefs for SEO research. Start with read-only access, check usage limits and permissions, and validate early answers against the reports you already trust.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI space is moving so fast it’s hard to believe that a year ago we still struggled to generate people with the correct amount of fingers 😂.

Industry observers note that the last couple of years have been pivotal for open source models and tools for artistic usage. AI tools for creative expression have never been more accessible, and we’re only scratching the surface. Join us as we look back at the key milestones, tools, and breakthroughs in AI & Arts from 2024, and forward for what’s to come in 2025 (spoiler 👀: we’re starting a fresh monthly roundup 👇).

According to recent reports, what were the standout releases of creative AI tools in 2024? We'll highlight the major releases across creative and artistic fields, with a particular focus on open-source developments in popular tasks like image and video generation.

Over 2 years since the OG stable diffusion was released and made waves in image generation with open source models, it’s now safe to say that when it comes to image generation from text, image editing and controlled image generation - open source models are giving closed source models a run for their money.

TD;LR - diffusion models and Gaussian flow matching are equivalent. Flow matching proposes a vector field parametrization of the network output that is different compared to the ones commonly used in diffusion models previously.

Back to practice: First to announce the shift was Stability AI with Stable Diffusion 3, however it was HunyuanDiT that became the first open source model with DiT architecture.This trend continued with the releases of AuraFlow, Flux.1 and Stable Diffusion 3.5.

Industry observers note that among many pivotal moments in the (not so long) history of open source image generation models, it’s safe to say that the release of Flux.1 was one of them. Flux [dev] achieved a new state-of-the-art, surpassing popular closed source models like Midjourney v6.0, DALL·E 3 (HD) on various benchmarks.

A positive side effect of advancements in image models is the significant improvement in personalization techniques for text-to-image models and controlled generation.

In a recent development, back in August 2022, transformative works like Textual Inversion and DreamBooth enhanced our ability to teach and introduce new concepts to text-to-image models, drastically expanding what could be done with them. These opened the door to a stream of improvements and enhancements building on top of these techniques (such as LoRA for diffusion models).

In a recent development, however, an upper bound to the quality of the fine-tuned models is naturally the base model from which it was fine-tuned. In that sense, we can’t neglect Stable Diffusion XL, which was also a significant marker in personalization for open source image generation models. A testimony to that is that even now, many of the popular techniques and models for personalization and controlled generation are based on SDXL. The advanced abilities of SDXL (and models that were released after with similar quality) together with the growing understanding of the semantic roles of different components in the diffusion model architecture raises the question - what can we achieve without further optimization?

cue in the rain of zero shot techniques - 2024 was definitely the year when generating high quality portraits from reference photos was made possible with as little as a single reference image & without any optimization. Training free techniques like IP adapter FaceID, InstantID, Photomaker and more came out and demonstrated competitive if not even superior abilities to those of fine-tuned models.

Similarly, image editing and controlled generation - such as image generation with canny / depth / pose constraints made progress too - both thanks to the growing quality of the base models and the community’s growing understanding of the semantic roles different components have (Instant Style, B-LoRA).

So what’s next? since the shift of paradigms to DiT and flow matching objectives, additional models came out trying to utilize DiT-based models like Flux and SD3.5 for similar purposes, but so far not quite beating the quality of the SDXL-based ones despite the superior quality of the underlying base model. This could be attributed to the relative lack of understanding of semantic roles of different components of the DiT compared to the Unet. 2025 could be the year when we identify those roles in DiTs as well, unlocking more possibilities with the next generation of image generation models.

As opposed to image generation, with video we still have a way to go. But, it’s safe to say that we’re very far away from where we were a year ago. While we’re all about open-source, the credit for (some) of the significant leap in AI video generation goes to OpenAI’s sora for changing our expectations of video model capabilities quite radically. And as fofr put nicely in AI video is having its Stable Diffusion moment (which we recommend reading 🙂) - it made everyone realize what is possible.

The recent surge of open-source video generation models, including CogVideoX, Mochi, Allegro, LTX Video, and HunyuanVideo, has also been noteworthy. Video generation is inherently more challenging than image generation due to the need for motion quality, coherence, and consistency. Additionally, video generation requires substantial computational and memory resources, leading to significant generation latency. This often hinders local usage, making many new open video models inaccessible to community hardware without extensive memory optimizations and quantization approaches that impact both inference latency and the quality of generated videos. Nevertheless the open source community has made remarkable progress - which was recently covered in this blog on the state of open video generation models.

While this implies that most community members are still unable to experiment and develop with open-source video models, it also suggests that we can expect significant advancements in 2025.

Recent findings suggest that audio generation has progressed significantly in the past year going from simple sounds to complete songs with lyrics. Despite challenges - Audio signals are complex and multifaceted, require more sophisticated mathematical models than models that generate text or images and training data quite scarce - 2024 saw open source releases like OuteTTS and IndicParlerTTS for text to speech and openai’s Whisper large v3 turbo for audio speech recognition. The year 2025 is already shaping up to be a breakthrough year for audio models, with a remarkable number of releases in January alone. We've seen the release of three fresh text-to-speech models: Kokoro, LLasa TTS and OuteTTS 0.3, as well as two new music models: JASCO and YuE. With this pace, we can expect even more exciting developments in the audio space throughout the year.

This song👇 was generated with YuE 🤯.

The beauty of open source is that it allows the community to experiment, find fresh usages for existing models / pipelines, improve on and build new tools together. Many of the creative AI tools that were popular this year are the fruit of joint community effort.

Here are some of our favorites:.

Many of the amazing Flux fine-tunes created in the last year were trained thanks to the AI-toolkit by ostris.

Inspired by fofr's face-to-many, Face to All combines the viral Instant ID model with added ControlNet depth constraints and community fine-tuned SDXL LoRAs to create training-free and high-quality portraits in creative stylizations.

Based on a ComfyUI workflow by Nathan Shipley, Flux style shaping combines Flux [dev] Redux and Flux [dev] Depth for style transfer and optical illusion creation.

Diffusers Image Outpaint makes use of the diffusers Stable Diffusion XL Fill Pipeline together with an SDXL union controlnet to seamlessly expand an input image.

Adding mimics to a static portrait was never easier with Live Portrait and Face Poke.

TRELLIS is a 3D generation model for versatile and high-quality 3D asset creation that took over the 3D landscape with a bang.

IC-Light, which stands for "Imposing Consistent Light", is a tool for relighting with foreground condition.

Industry observers note that 2025 is the year for open-source to catch up on video, movement, and audio models, making room for more modalities. With advancements in efficient computing and quantization, we can expect significant leaps in open-source video models. As we approach a (natural) plateau in image generation models, we can shift our focus to other tasks and modalities.

It has been revealed that yuE - series of open-source music foundation models for full song generation. YuE is possibly the best open source model for music generation (with an Apache 2.0 license!), achieving competitive results to closed source models like Suno.

try it out & read more: demo, model weights.

Hunyuan 3D-2 , SPAR3D, DiffSplat - 3D generation models. 3D models are coming in hot - not long after the release of TRELLIS, Hunyuan 3D-2, SPAR3D and DiffSplat are here to take over the 3D landscape.

In a recent development, lumina-Image 2.0 - text to image model. Lumina is a 2B parameter model competitive with the 12B Flux.1 [dev] and with an Apache 2.0 license(!!).

try it out & read more: demo, model weights.

ComfyUI-to-Gradio - a step-by-step guide on how to convert a complex ComfyUI workflow to a simple Gradio application, and how to deploy this application on Hugging Face Spaces ZeroGPU serverless structure, which allows for it to be deployed and run for free in a serverless manner read more here.

In a recent development, kicking off with this blog, we (Poli & Linoy) will be bringing you a monthly roundup of the latest in the creative AI world. In such a fast-evolving space, it’s tough to stay on top of all the latest developments, let alone sift through them. That’s where we come in & hopefully this way we can make creative AI tools more accessible.

Thanks for the great blog post. I am looking forward to seeing the next concern!

📻 🎙️ Hey, I made a podcast about this blog post, check it out!

This podcast is generated via ngxson/kokoro-podcast-generator, using DeepSeek-R1 and Kokoro-TTS.

Industry observers note that really enjoyed reading The AI Tools for Art Newsletter—such a well-structured and insightful overview of major AI-driven creative tools in 2024! The breakdown of image generation, personalization, and video generation was particularly helpful in understanding how AI is transforming artistic workflows.

While researching, I found this resource on AI-powered image generation with RunPod and ComfyUI, which covers ComfyUI setup, diffusion model workflows, and Hugging Face model integration: https://mobisoftinfotech.com/resources/blog/flux-on-runpod-using-comfyui.

Would love to hear your thoughts on how AI’s role in stylization and personalization might evolve in 2025!

Mini-R1: Reproduce Deepseek R1 „aha moment“ a RL tutorial

  • The release of Deepseek R1 shocked the industry.
  • According to recent reports, in the paper they described an "aha moment" when using pure RL to train the model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This post was written by Philipp Schmid and orginially posted on philschmid.de code can found here.

The release of Deepseek R1 shocked the industry. Why? Well, DeepSeek-R1 is an open model that rivals OpenAI's o1 in complex reasoning tasks, introduced using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and RL-focused multi-stage training approach. They not only released the model, but also a research paper on how they did it.

According to recent reports, in the paper they described an "aha moment" when using pure RL to train the model. During this phase, DeepSeek-R1-Zero (the first test of DeepSeek-R1) learns to allocate more thinking time to a problem by reevaluating its initial approach without any human feedback or data describing how to do it. They describe this as an "aha moment" as:.

This behavior is not only a testament to the model’s growing reasoning abilities but also a captivating example of how reinforcement learning can lead to unexpected and sophisticated outcomes.

Industry observers note that in this blog post we want to recreate the small "aha moment" of DeepSeek-R1 using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and the Countdown Game. We will train an open model using reinforcement learning trying to teach it self-verification and search abilities all on its own to solve the Countdown Game. The Countdown game is a numbers puzzle where players use a set of randomly drawn numbers and basic arithmetic operations (+, -, ×, ÷) to reach or get as close as possible to a target number.

Recent findings suggest that the blog post focuses on training distributed training using Deepspeed and vLLM. It was run on a 4x NVIDIA H100 GPUs.

Note: This blog is inspired by Jiayi Pan who initially explored the idea and proofed it with a small model.

But Before we start, let's take a look at the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and understand how it works.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is a reinforcement learning algorithm to improve the reasoning capabilities of LLMs. It was introduced in the DeepSeekMath paper in the context of mathematical reasoning. GRPO modifies the traditional Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) by eliminating the need for a value function model. Instead, it estimates baselines from group scores, reducing memory usage and computational overhead. GRPO, now also used by the Qwen team, can be used with rule/binary-based Rewards as well as General Reward Models to improve models on helpfulness.

Recent findings suggest that our first step is to install Hugging Face Libraries and Pytorch, vllm, and trl, transformers and datasets. If you haven't heard of trl yet, don't worry. It is a latest library on top of transformers and datasets, which makes it easier to fine-tune, rlhf, align open LLMs.

Note: you may need to restart the kernel to use updated packages.

Sources indicate that we are going to use the Jiayi-Pan/Countdown-Tasks-3to4 dataset, which contains samples with 3 to 4 numbers and solutions. As Model we are going to use Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct which is a 3B parameter instruction tuned model. This makes it easier to showcase the "aha moment" as it already can follow instructions. Jiayi-Pan explored that the model needs to have a certain quality to be able to learn the reasoning process, starting with > 1.5B parameters.

According to recent reports, TRL supports Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) through a dedicated GRPOTrainer for aligning LLMs from preference data, as described in DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models. The GRPOTrainer is a subclass of the Trainer from the transformers library and supports all the same features, including logging, checkpointing, distributed training, and parameter efficient fine-tuning (PEFT).

In a recent development, the GRPOTrainer supports generic Outcome Reward Models (ORM) and custom reward functions, that can be used to implement Rule-Based Reward Models. In the Deepseek R1 paper they implemented Rule-Based Reward Models to verify the correctness of the generated solutions. In our exmaple we are going to do a similar approach, where we will create 2 reward functions that:.

Note: Correct in our example includes the equation, for example 55 + 36 - 7 - 19.

According to recent reports, hugging Face TRL added support for distributed training with Deepspeed and using vLLM for faster generation. I preprared a run_r1_grpo.py script and a receipes/grpo-qwen-2.5-3b-deepseek-r1-countdown.yaml config file to run the training.

This configuration is tested and validated on a Node with 4x H100 80GBs, where a single step takes around 45-60s, as we can leverage vLLM for generation and DeepSpeed for distributed training. Therefore we need to make sure we correctly set the num_processes to the number of GPUs you have - 1 as the last one will be used with vLLM for Generation. If you are using more GPUS you need to change the vllm_device in the config file to last index GPU, e.g. if you have 8 GPUs you need to set vllm_device=7 and your num_processes to 7.

With the optimized distributed training a single step with 8 generations per sample on 4x H100 80GBs takes around 45-60s. The full training for 450 steps takes around 6 hours.

The script saves random completions to the completion_samples folder, which you can use to inspect the model's progress. It includes completion_samples.txt and success_completion_samples.txt. The completion_samples.txt includes all completions, while the success_completion_samples.txt which correctly solves the equation. Below you can find the interesating training obeserations on how the performance changes over time, as well as the Tensornoard logs and successfull reasoning samples.

The model with checkpoints for every 25th step can be found at philschmid/qwen-2.5-3b-r1-countdown.

Recent findings suggest that I started the experiment using the hyperparameters from the DeepSeekMath paper with a learning rate of 1e-6 and a beta (KL coefficient) of 0.04, which led to unstable training runs after around 150 steps. I ran some small ablations and decreased both the learning rate to 5e-7 and the beta to 0.001, based on a test from OpenRLHF. I coulnd't test how increasing the num_generations from 8 to 64 would affect the training. 64 is the generation value, which was used in the DeepSeekMath paper. All other parameters can be found in the grpo-qwen-2.5-3b-deepseek-r1-countdown.yaml config file.

I have 3 potential assumptions why the model shifts from "word reasoning" to "programmatic execution":.

According to recent reports, the release of DeepSeek R1 and its research paper might be a breakpoint for open-science and open-source development. Just a week after the DeepSeek release, we've been able to reproduce a simple version of R1 learned "reasoning" using GRPO and the Countdown Game. While our implementation focuses on a specific task rather than general reasoning and convergence into a very specific "reasoning" format, it shows that the method is working.

Looking in to 2025, it's clear that we are on the cusp of even more significant progress. RL will become more accessible and user-friendly, more researchers and developers will explore its potential, but also require amount of more compute as before and compared to supervised fine-tuning.

I am excited for 2025. If you have any questions or ideas, feel free to reach out to me.

If this sounds interesting, we’d love your help! Whether it’s contributing code, joining discussions on Hugging Face.

How Developers Can Improve Their Learning and Productivity With AI

📖 0% read

Industry observers note that artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how developers learn, write code, and manage their daily work. Tasks that once required hours of searching, testing, and manual effort can now be completed with help from AI. Developers can use it to understand complex programming concepts, find coding errors, learn fresh technologies, and complete repetitive tasks.

However, AI is not only useful for writing code faster. It can also help developers improve their technical knowledge, solve problems, and build better learning habits. When used correctly, it can become a useful assistant throughout the software development process.

The key is to understand where AI can help and where human skills are still needed. Here are several practical ways developers can use AI to improve their learning and productivity.

Recent findings suggest that learning a new programming language or understanding a difficult concept can take time. Developers often need to read long explanations, watch tutorials, and test different examples before they understand how something works.

Industry observers note that AI can make this process easier by explaining technical concepts in simple language. Instead of searching through several websites, developers can ask direct questions and receive explanations based on their current knowledge.

Sources indicate that for example, a developer learning JavaScript can ask AI to explain promises, callbacks, or asynchronous functions. It can break these topics into smaller parts and provide simple code examples to make them easier to understand.

Another useful approach is to ask AI to explain the same concept in different ways. If one explanation is difficult to understand, a different example or comparison may make the idea clearer.

Recent findings suggest that AI explanations are not always accurate, especially when dealing with complex programming concepts or unfamiliar technologies. Developers should verify key information before using it in their projects. Hallucination detection can help identify fabricated facts, incorrect technical explanations, and misleading information in AI-generated responses, making it easier to check the accuracy of what they learn.

This helps developers spend less time struggling with unfamiliar topics and more time building their technical knowledge.

Software development changes regularly. Newly introduced frameworks, libraries, programming languages, and development methods continue to appear. Developers need to keep learning if they want to stay up to date.

AI can support this process by helping developers create learning plans based on their goals and current skills.

Recent findings suggest that for example, a developer who wants to learn Python can ask AI to create a beginner-friendly learning plan. The plan can include basic syntax, variables, loops, functions, object-oriented programming, and small projects.

Sources indicate that AI can also recommend practical exercises for each topic. Instead of only reading about a programming concept, developers can write code and test their understanding.

Here are some ways to use AI when learning new technologies:.

However, developers should not depend entirely on AI-generated explanations. They should also read official documentation and test examples themselves. This helps them understand how technologies work in real development environments.

AI can help developers improve their coding skills by providing examples, explaining different solutions, and identifying areas that need improvement.

For example, a developer may write a function that works but contains unnecessary steps. They can ask AI to review the code and suggest ways to make it easier to read, maintain, or understand.

Industry observers note that AI can also explain why one solution may be better than another. This allows developers to learn different approaches instead of always following the first solution they find.

Some practical ways to use AI for coding improvement include:.

It has been revealed that developers can also ask AI to create small coding challenges based on their skill level. For example, someone learning Python can request exercises about lists, dictionaries, loops, and functions.

Recent findings suggest that the important thing is to understand the code instead of copying it without review. Developers who examine the logic behind each solution can improve their programming knowledge over time.

Recent findings suggest that developers learn fresh information from many sources, including online courses, technical blogs, documentation, tutorials, and coding projects. Without a proper system, it can become difficult to find useful information when they need it again.

AI can help developers organize this knowledge and make learning resources easier to review.

According to recent reports, for example, developers can use AI to summarize long technical explanations, create revision questions, and organize important programming concepts into smaller topics. They can also turn their learning notes into structured study guides that make it easier to revisit important information.

According to recent reports, A well-organized knowledge system can be useful when learning a fresh framework or preparing for technical interviews. Instead of searching through old browser tabs or reading the same documentation repeatedly, developers can return to their saved explanations and notes.

Here are some useful ways to organize technical knowledge:.

Sources indicate that technical documentation can contain detailed explanations that are difficult to remember. Developers can use AI to summarize important sections and turn them into short notes.

For example, when learning a newly introduced API, they can save information about its main functions, parameters, common errors, and practical examples.

Reading information does not always mean remembering it. Developers can ask AI to create questions from their notes so they can test their understanding.

For example, after learning about database indexing, they can create questions about how indexes work, when to use them, and how they affect query performance.

Developers should also save important information about their projects. This may include coding decisions, API details, database structures, and solutions to common problems.

Keeping these details organized makes it easier to return to a project after a break or help another developer understand the work.

According to recent reports, developers spend a large part of their working time on tasks that do not always require complex problem-solving. These may include writing basic code structures, creating test cases, preparing documentation, and handling repeated coding patterns.

AI can help reduce this manual effort by generating suggestions and automating parts of these tasks.

It has been revealed that for example, when starting a latest project, developers often need to create similar code structures, such as basic functions, configuration files, and reusable components. An AI coding assistant can generate an initial version that developers can review and adjust.

Automating these activities gives developers more time to focus on notable parts of their projects, such as system design, complex features, and problem-solving.

However, generated code should always be checked before it is added to a project. Developers need to make sure it follows project requirements, coding standards, and security rules.

It has been revealed that finding and fixing bugs is an vital part of software development. Even experienced developers can spend hours trying to understand why a program is not working as expected.

AI can help make debugging easier by explaining error messages, identifying possible causes, and suggesting solutions.

For example, when a developer encounters a Python error, they can share the relevant code and error message with an AI assistant. The assistant can explain what the error means and suggest possible ways to fix it.

Recent findings suggest that AI can also help developers review code before submitting it. It may identify common problems such as:.

Another useful approach is to ask AI to explain why a particular bug occurs instead of only requesting a corrected version of the code.

This helps developers understand the problem and avoid making the same mistake in future projects.

Still, AI suggestions are not always correct. Developers should test proposed fixes, review the surrounding code, and confirm that the solution does not introduce newly introduced problems.

Managing several development tasks at once can be difficult. Developers may need to work on upcoming features, fix bugs, review code, attend meetings, and meet project deadlines.

AI can help organize these responsibilities by breaking large tasks into smaller and more manageable steps.

Sources indicate that for example, if a developer needs to build a user authentication system, they can ask AI to divide the work into separate tasks. These may include creating registration forms, setting up database tables, implementing login logic, adding password protection, and testing the system.

This makes it easier to understand the work involved and decide what needs attention first.

AI can also help explain technical requirements before development begins. This may reduce confusion and help developers identify missing details early.

Industry observers note that however, AI-generated intends should be treated as starting points. Developers still need to consider their actual deadlines, technical limitations, and project requirements before following them.

Although AI offers many benefits, depending on it for every programming task can affect a developer's ability to solve problems independently.

If developers always ask AI to write code, fix errors, and explain every concept, they may miss opportunities to develop their own technical skills.

A 2026 Anthropic study found that participants using AI scored 17 percentage points lower on a programming knowledge quiz than participants who worked without AI in the experiment. This highlights why understanding the work still matters when using coding assistants.

Developers can avoid excessive dependence on AI by following a few simple practices:.

Recent findings suggest that when facing a coding problem, spend some time understanding it and trying possible solutions. If you get stuck, use AI to explore the problem rather than asking it to complete everything.

Industry observers note that never add AI-generated code to a project without understanding what it does. Review the logic, check the functions, and test the output.

Industry observers note that AI can sometimes provide outdated information, incorrect code, or explanations that do not fit a particular project. Check key details against official documentation and reliable technical resources.

Regular coding practice without assistance helps developers maintain their problem-solving skills. It also indicates whether they truly understand a programming concept.

The best approach is to use AI as a helpful assistant while keeping independent thinking and technical judgment at the center of development work.

Using AI occasionally can be helpful, but developers can get more value from it by making it part of a regular learning and working routine.

A simple daily routine can help developers balance their project responsibilities with continuous learning.

For example, developers can follow this approach:.

Start with a learning goal: Spend some time understanding a new programming concept, framework, or technology. Use AI to explain difficult topics and provide practical examples.

Initiative the day's development tasks: Ask AI to help organize notable tasks and break complex work into smaller steps.

According to recent reports, use AI during development: Get help with unfamiliar code, debugging, test cases, and repetitive tasks. Review all suggestions before using them.

Save useful information: Keep vital explanations, coding examples, and solutions in an organized knowledge base for future reference.

Review what you learned: At the end of the day, revisit notable concepts and test your understanding through small questions or coding exercises.

Developers do not need to spend hours following this routine. Even a short period of focused learning each day can help them build knowledge while managing their regular development work.

According to recent reports, AI is becoming a useful part of modern software development. It can help developers understand difficult concepts, learn latest technologies, improve code quality, debug problems, and complete repetitive tasks more efficiently.

It has been revealed that however, better productivity does not simply mean writing more code in less time. Developers also need to understand what they are building, improve their problem-solving skills, and keep learning as technology changes.

According to recent reports, the most effective approach is to use AI for support rather than letting it make every decision. By combining AI assistance with regular practice, independent thinking, and organized learning, developers can improve both their technical skills and everyday productivity.
